nameStory: The name 'cinquefoil' comes from the French words 'cinq' (five) and 'feuille' (leaf), referring to the characteristic five leaflets found on many plants in this group. It's called 'tall' cinquefoil because it stands notably taller than its low-growing cousins that hug the ground. The 'sticky' nickname comes from the glandular hairs that make the stem feel tacky to the touch.
description: Tall cinquefoil is a sturdy perennial wildflower that stands out from other cinquefoils by growing upright instead of creeping along the ground. This member of the rose family typically reaches 1-3 feet tall, with a branching stem topped by clusters of small white or cream-colored flowers. The compound leaves are divided into several toothed leaflets, giving the plant a somewhat feathery appearance. Unlike many of its relatives, this cinquefoil has a distinctly upright, almost shrub-like growth habit.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows tall and upright (1-3 feet) rather than creeping along the ground like most other cinquefoils, with a sturdy, branching stem that feels sticky when touched

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to cream-colored flowers with five rounded petals arranged in branched clusters at the top of the plant, blooming in summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 5-9 toothed leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, with a slightly fuzzy texture and grayish-green color

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Stems feel noticeably sticky or glandular when rubbed between fingers, covered with fine hairs that trap moisture and small particles

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dry seeds in clusters where the flowers were, each tiny seed less than 2mm long

habitat: Look for tall cinquefoil in dry, open areas like prairies, meadows, and rocky slopes throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained soils and full sun, often growing alongside other prairie plants and grasses. This species is relatively uncommon in the region, preferring the drier conditions found in natural openings and disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as compound leaflets, and the plant begins its upward growth from the base.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with clusters of small white flowers at the top of sturdy stems, making identification easiest during this season.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and produce dry seed clusters, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to the ground, surviving as underground roots until spring returns.

funFact: This plant was recently 'relocated' botanically - it used to be classified in the genus Potentilla with hundreds of other cinquefoils, but DNA studies revealed it was different enough to deserve its own special genus, Drymocallis, making it feel like a botanical VIP with its own exclusive club!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other cinquefoils, but remember the height difference - if it's standing tall and sticky, it's likely tall cinquefoil, while if it's creeping along the ground, it's probably a different species. The upright growth habit is your best clue.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents an interesting example of how plant classification changes as we learn more - many field guides still list it under the old genus Potentilla, so don't be confused if you see it called 'Potentilla arguta' in older books.
compareHints: Since tall cinquefoil is the only Drymocallis species in New England, compare it to other rose family members like the low-growing cinquefoils (Potentilla species) which creep along the ground, or wild strawberries which have three leaflets instead of five or more. The upright growth habit and sticky stems make tall cinquefoil unique among New England's cinquefoil relatives.
